claims.text: Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported yield strength of 786 MPa.
Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
Untreated HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported terminal strain of 13.5%.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has limited tensile ductility.
HfZrTiTa0.53 should receive a post-fabrication deep cryogenic treatment before final thermal processing.
Deep cryogenic treatment will induce a beneficial phase transition in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Deep cryogenic treatment will refine the microstructure of HfZrTiTa0.53.
Deep cryogenic treatment will reduce residual stresses in HfZrTiTa0.53.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a predominantly BCC matrix.
Deep cryogenic treatment may produce minor FCC-like features in the predominantly BCC HfZrTiTa0.53 matrix.
The proposed phase transition and microstructural refinement will provide additional or more active slip systems.
Additional slip mechanisms will make tensile plastic deformation more uniform.
Deep cryogenic treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation by approximately 20–50%, from an asserted 13.5% baseline to roughly 16–20% or more.
Deep cryogenic treatment will retain yield strength near the 786 MPa baseline.
Deep cryogenic treatment will retain compressive strength near the 1314 MPa baseline.
Deep cryogenic treatment will preserve impact-triggered energy release during penetration.
The predicted ductility benefit applies at room temperature under tensile loading at a moderate mechanical-test strain rate.
In Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr, deep cryogenic treatment increased final tensile strength by 25% relative to the as-cast alloy and 11% relative to the as-deposited alloy.
In Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr, deep cryogenic treatment increased elongation by 48% relative to the as-cast alloy and 10% relative to the as-deposited alloy.
Deep cryogenic treatment induced a phase transition without additional deformation in the cited Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr alloy.

contradictions.description: The reported 13.5% value is identified as terminal strain, but the prediction treats it as the baseline uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain and uniform tensile elongation are not interchangeable metrics.

The hypothesis requires both improved elongation and retention of strength and impact energy, but the stated falsification rule requires inadequate elongation concurrently with retention of the other properties. Thus, a substantial loss of strength or impact energy may fail to falsify the hypothesis under the rule even though it contradicts the prediction.
